notes: 12-species starting list: 6 edible, 6 toxic. Covers most common Central Texas encounters and their critical look-alike pairs. inat_taxon_id values verified via iNaturalist API (GET /v1/taxa/{id}) 2026-06-04. Note: mahonia_trifoliolata is stored under its synonym Berberis trifoliolata in iNaturalist (taxon 273862).

distinguishing_features: Compound leaves with 5-11 leaflets
Flat-topped white flower clusters (cymes)
Small dark purple/black berries in dense flat clusters
Woody stems, gray-brown bark with white lenticels
Opposite branching pattern
species.habitat: Moist areas, stream banks, woodland edges
species.notes: Berries safe cooked; raw berries can cause nausea. Leaves, bark, roots toxic.

distinguishing_features: Forked tendrils (2-branched)
Deeply lobed or heart-shaped leaves, white-woolly underside
Dark purple to black berries, 2-4 seeds per berry
Tight clustered bunches on woody vine
Tart, thick-skinned berries
species.notes: Very astringent raw — often used for jelly/wine. Sap can irritate skin.

distinguishing_features: Trailing (not upright) thorny canes
Compound leaves with 3-5 leaflets
White 5-petaled flowers
Aggregate drupelets (like a blackberry), black when ripe
Grows low to ground — trailing habit distinguishes from blackberry
species.habitat: Open fields, roadsides, woodland edges, disturbed areas
species.notes: One of earliest spring fruits in Central Texas.

distinguishing_features: Vivid magenta/purple berry clusters tightly encircling the stem at leaf nodes
Large opposite leaves, soft and slightly fuzzy
Berries arranged in tight whorls around stem (not at branch tips)
Shrub form, 3-8 feet tall
White/pink flowers before berry stage
species.habitat: Woodland understory, moist to dry woods
species.notes: Berries bland raw, better as jelly. Primary distinguishing: stem-encircling berry arrangement.

distinguishing_features: Holly-like trifoliate leaves with sharp spiny lobes
Bright red berries (unique color for Hill Country)
Evergreen shrub 3-6 feet tall
Yellow flowers in late winter/early spring
Berries ripen in spring — unusual early season
species.habitat: Rocky limestone hillsides, cedar-oak woodland, caliche soils
species.notes: Very tart, high in vitamin C. Classic Hill Country foraging target. No dangerous look-alikes. iNaturalist indexes this species as Berberis trifoliolata (taxonomic synonym).

distinguishing_features: Small orange-red to dark purple single drupes on long thin stalks
Berries single, not clustered
Distinctive warty/corky gray bark
Asymmetric leaf base (hallmark feature)
Berries have single hard seed, thin sweet flesh
species.habitat: Stream banks, bottomlands, urban areas, fence rows
species.notes: Very common urban/suburban tree in Central Texas. No dangerous look-alikes.

distinguishing_features: Thick magenta/hot-pink stems when mature (key identifier)
Simple large oval leaves (up to 10+ inches) — NOT compound
Berries in elongated grape-like racemes on vivid pink-red stems
Large herbaceous plant (4-10 feet), dies back in winter
Massive white taproot (toxic)
species.notes: ALL parts toxic, especially roots and unripe berries. Ripe berries less toxic but still dangerous. Causes severe GI distress and potentially fatal respiratory depression.

distinguishing_features: Single crescent/moon-shaped seed (cross-section looks like crescent — key identifier)
Simple (not compound) tendrils or no tendrils
Peltate leaf attachment (stem attaches inside leaf margin, not at edge)
Berries in loose clusters, less dense than grape
Leaves less lobed than grape, more shield-shaped
species.notes: Fatal look-alike for wild grape. Seed shape is definitive but requires cutting berry open. Do not rely on seed check alone in the field. Texas-rare (23 iNat obs) — scrape globally for training data.

species.priority_reason: Common, easily confused with dewberry at young stage
distinguishing_features: Simple (not compound) leaves with wavy margins
Small star-shaped white flowers with yellow anthers (Solanum pattern)
Berries in small umbel-like clusters, turn black when ripe
Non-thorny smooth herbaceous stems
Much smaller plant than dewberry, no trailing canes
species.habitat: Disturbed areas, gardens, waste ground, crop fields
species.notes: Toxic — solanine. Ripe black berries less toxic than unripe green berries. Some cultures cook ripe berries but this is NOT recommended without expert guidance.

species.priority_reason: Attractive berries often misidentified as edible
distinguishing_features: Deciduous holly — berries persist on bare branches after leaf drop (distinctive)
Bright red-orange berries clustered along stems
Alternate leaves with serrated margins
Berries do NOT have calyx star on bottom (unlike persimmon)
Shrub to small tree form
species.notes: Berries toxic — ilicin. Often confused for a food source due to bright color and winter persistence.

distinguishing_features: Evergreen shrub/small tree with small oval serrated leaves
Bright red berries in dense clusters along stems
Leaves smaller and more rounded than possumhaw
Very common landscape and native plant in Texas
Leaves contain caffeine (leaves historically used for tea — NOT berries)
species.habitat: Woodland understory, urban landscapes, coastal to central Texas
species.notes: Berries toxic. Note: leaves contain caffeine and were historically used as a tea by Indigenous peoples — ONLY leaves, NEVER berries.

distinguishing_features: Bipinnately compound leaves (large, feathery — twice divided)
Yellow-tan berries in loose drooping clusters, persist after leaf drop
Berries wrinkle and turn yellowish-tan when ripe
Strong smell when berries are crushed
Medium to large tree form — invasive across Texas
species.habitat: Urban areas, disturbed land, roadsides, stream banks
species.notes: Toxic — tetranortriterpene neurotoxins. 6-8 berries potentially fatal to a child. Rapid acting. Common urban tree — high accidental exposure risk.
